deleted.text: This note describes how the Lumen app proves to the backend who the signed-in user is.
It covers the format of the access token, how the gateway validates it, how sign-in and sign-out work, and what the app does when a token is refused.
An access token is an opaque string of 32 random bytes, encoded in base64url, that carries no meaning of its own.
The auth service stores a SHA-256 hash of each token as one row of the sessions table, together with the user identifier, the device identifier, the granted scopes and an expiry time.
A token stays valid for 30 days after its last use, because every accepted request moves its expiry forward by 30 days.
The app therefore never has to renew a token while the user keeps opening it at least once a month.
Every request from the app reaches the API gateway first.
The gateway hashes the bearer token and looks the hash up in the sessions table.
If no row matches, the gateway answers 401 and the request goes no further.
If the row has expired, the gateway deletes it and answers 401.
If the row is valid, the gateway moves its expiry time forward and adds the user identifier and the scopes as the X-Lumen-User and X-Lumen-Scopes headers.
Services behind the gateway trust these two headers and never see the token itself.
Each service checks that the scopes in X-Lumen-Scopes include the scope its endpoint needs and answers 403 otherwise.
The gateway keeps a 10-second in-memory cache of recent lookups, so that a burst of requests from one screen costs a single database read.
The app signs in with the user's email and a one-time code, or with Sign in with Apple or Google.
On success the auth service creates a token, writes its row into the sessions table and returns the token once in the response body.
A user may hold up to ten sessions at once, one per device.
Signing in on an eleventh device deletes the session that was used least recently.
Sign-out deletes the row of the current token from the sessions table, and the token stops working as soon as the gateway cache entry expires.
The account page also offers "Sign out everywhere", which deletes every row of the user.
Support staff can end all sessions of a user from the admin console when an account is reported as compromised.
The app keeps the token in the iOS Keychain or the Android Keystore.
Logs, crash reports and analytics events carry a redacted placeholder wherever a token would appear.
Deletes the stored token and shows the sign-in screen
A 401 always means the session is gone, so the app does not retry the request.
The sessions table lives in the main Postgres cluster and holds about 4 million rows.
A nightly job removes the rows whose expiry time has passed.
Gateway latency is dominated by the lookup, which adds about 3 ms at the median and 20 ms at the 99th percentile.
The identity team is paged when the lookup error rate stays above 1 percent for five minutes.
The local stack starts the auth service with an empty sessions table and a seed user.
Integration tests sign in through the real endpoint and reuse the returned token for the whole suite.

candidates.sentence: A request made with an access token leaves its expiry time where it was rather than pushing it forward.
An access token never carries the user's name, email address or phone number.
The gateway no longer looks up the sessions table before it forwards a request.
If the signature does not verify or the token has expired, the service answers 401.
Services cache the published keys for one hour and fetch them again when a token names a key identifier they do not know.
Services no longer wait on a round trip to the auth service before they serve a request.
The app reads the expiry time from the token's claims instead of keeping a countdown timer of its own.
Lumen does not take that option, and each successful refresh returns a new refresh token and retires the one that was sent.
The Lumen app keeps both of its tokens in the iOS Keychain and the Android Keystore, never in those plain stores.
The auth service signs with one active key and publishes it together with the previous key.
A new key pair is generated every 90 days, and the previous key stays published for one day after the switch.
Keys are rotated on that fixed calendar as a routine step rather than as a response to an incident.
If the refresh endpoint cannot be reached, the app keeps the user signed in and retries with a backoff capped at one minute.
